planting.note: Root softwood cuttings in early summer or set out container-grown plants in well-drained, moist to average soil in full sun; this selection blooms on old wood, so prune immediately after flowering rather than in fall or winter.

directions: June Bride is a heavy-flowering selection of Nippon spirea, chosen for producing a noticeably denser, more continuous cover of white button-like flower clusters along its arching stems than the straight species typically offers. Its bloom season also runs somewhat longer than average for the species, extending the white floral display into early summer before the dark blue-green foliage takes over as the main feature. The rounded, mounding habit and overall size are similar to the species, fitting the same foundation, border, and mass-planting roles. Shear lightly right after flowering to keep the mound tidy, since old-wood bloomers set next year's buds soon after their spring flush finishes.

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, sheltered from strong wind and the hottest afternoon sun that can scorch the variegated margins.

directions: This is a slow-growing, more compact sport of giant dogwood, prized above all for foliage rather than flower: broad leaves are irregularly margined in creamy white over gray-green centers, brightening the same dramatically horizontal, tiered branching that gives the species its architectural silhouette. Flat corymbs of small white flowers open in early summer atop the foliage layers, followed by small blue-black fruit, but both are secondary to the season-long variegated display. Because reduced chlorophyll makes the leaf margins prone to scorch, site it out of hot midday sun and drying wind, and keep soil evenly moist, especially while the tree establishes. It earned the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit and is widely regarded as one of the finest variegated specimen trees for a partly shaded lawn or woodland-edge setting with room to display its tiered form.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder — Cornus controversa

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Art's Pride was one of the first named hybrids to bring warm orange tones into garden coneflowers.

directions: Art's Pride was bred by Dr. Jim Ault at the Chicago Botanic Garden as part of the Meadowbrite breeding program and later marketed under the trademark Orange Meadowbrite. It is an early cross of Echinacea purpurea and the naturally yellow-flowered E. paradoxa, producing warm burnt-orange, gently outward-facing petals around a coppery-brown cone rather than the drooping form typical of most species coneflowers. Plant in full sun in lean to average, well-drained soil, where established clumps handle heat and drought with ease. Deadhead through summer to prolong bloom, or leave the last flush of seed heads standing into fall and winter to feed goldfinches; divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Introduction Program
